newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan investment in China seen cooling - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan investment in China seen cooling - analysts.

text.p: The "mainland fever" of some Taiwan firms may be cooling after two industrial giants scuttled huge China projects, but analysts say the government must work harder if it wants to keep their capital working in Taiwan.

Taiwan food company President Enterprises said on Thursday it had abandoned plans to build a US$100 million power plant on the Chinese mainland and instead would invest more than T$30 billion (US$1.1 billion) in local projects over two years.
"We hope our own company can continue to develop in Taiwan," President vice chairman Kao Ching-yuan said on state radio. "We have decided to keep our roots here."

President is Taiwan's top investor in China, with US$200 million tied up in 15 mainland companies. But spokesman Yang Yu-pao told Reuters the company was unwilling to give its mainland partners a controlling interest in the project.
"President Enterprises cannot reach agreement with mainland China's counterparts, so we decided to abandon the planned US$100 million power project," Yang said.
President said in August it would delay its application to build a power plant in the central Chinese city of Wuhan until Taiwan set out clearer guidelines on mainland investments.

The move followed Formosa Plastics Group's August 16 announcement that it was ending a deal to build what would have been the biggest Taiwanese project in China to date, a US$3 billion power plant project in coastal Fujian province.
Analysts said the two conglomerates' dramatic reversals were likely to chill other Taiwanese firms' plans to invest in China, at least for the time being.
"The moves by Formosa and President will slow other companies' plans to invest in China," said Allen Huang, chief dealer of Baring Securities.
"Other firms will wonder: 'If this is not a good time for companies like Formosa and President, it may not be a good time for them either'," Huang said.
President Enterprises said it would spend more than T$30 billion in the next two years to build two shopping malls and to enter medical manufacturing.
The malls would be in southern Kaohsiung and Tainan cities. The pharmaceutical project would involve an investment of T$900 million (US$33 million).

Chung Chin, an investment expert at Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, said the government would have to try harder to persuade local companies to keep making investments in Taiwan rather than China, Taiwan's political arch rival.

"It is clear the government wants to convince local companies not to forget which side they belong (to)," Chung said. "But if it wants the businesses to stay forever, it needs more than just moral persuasion."
President Lee Teng-hui said in August that the island needed to review its policy of targeting China as its main market to avoid over-dependence on the mainland for investment.

Taiwan and China were divided by the Chinese civil war in 1949. All Taiwanese investments in China now require government approval, but Taipei remains concerned that its economy may become too dependent on China, and thus politically vulnerable.
Some 30,000 Taiwanese companies have poured more than US$20 billion into China since a political thaw in the late 1980s.
But Kao Koong-lian, spokesman for Taiwan's top mainland policy-making body, warned local businessmen on Thursday to be cautious when considering investments in China.
"Do not put all your eggs in one basket," Kao was quoted as saying by the state-funded Central News Agency.
